Task 12.0: Sulfur TES Design Review (M-3.12.1, M-3.12.2) Element 16 received an independent review of sulfur TES design from Bill Huffman, Director of Quality and Engineering at Ward Vessel and Exchanger. He is also a chairman of TEMA technical committee. The review report did not identify any major issues. One key recommendation, echoing a suggestion from Shane Powers at the DOE, was the non-destructive examination of the internal heat exchanger coil. This examination was successfully carried out using a helium leak test, as discussed in Task 12. Other recommendations, such as spot x-ray of welds on the vessel and the installation of manway/inspection openings, will be incorporated into future systems that Element 16 develops for commercial installations. Significant Accomplishments and Conclusions: Element 16 successfully completed a comprehensive set of research and product development activities, including corrosion and mechanical durability testing to identify materials compatible with molten sulfur, thermo-fluidic characterization and design studies of sulfur TES using simulation tools validated with lab prototype data to optimize molten sulfur TES design operating up to 300 oC. Building on these activities, Element 16 team successfully set up, commissioned, and demonstrated pilot sulfur thermal energy storage system at its facility. Although the original plan called for pilot prototype testing at a host site, Element 16 was unable to secure a signed agreement. The original solar thermal partner’s outlet temperature (<200 °C) was insufficient to meet project goals, and other prospective site partners were unable to commit due to scheduling uncertainties. Additionally, rising steel prices since project initiation introduced budget pressures that required renegotiation of performance metrics. To address these challenges, Element 16 proposed modifying the pilot scope to complete the testing activities in-house using simulated solar thermal profiles, while still meeting the originally negotiated performance metrics. This pivot enabled the team to maximize technical progress despite site and cost constraints, and the plan was formally reviewed and approved by DOE. The pilot sulfur TES system was fully characterized in terms of average charge and discharge rates and round-trip efficiency. The unit underwent multiple charge-discharge cycles and was operated at a maximum heat transfer fluid inlet temperature of 295 oC and a bulk sulfur temperature of 285 oC, without any safety issues throughout the testing campaign. The thermal-to-thermal round-trip efficiency was calculated to be 85%. As system size increases (larger tank diameter), higher thermal-to-thermal round-trip efficiency can be achieved due to a decrease in surface area to volume ratio, with a resulting reduction in heat losses per unit storage capacity. The experimental results collectively validate the system's capability to operate effectively under intermittent charging conditions, a key requirement for integrating with variable renewable energy sources like solar thermal.
